newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen premier designate forms new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Yemen premier designate forms new cabinet.

text.p: Yemen's prime minister-designate Faraj Said Bin Ghanem, an independent economist from the south, formed a new government on Thursday, state-run television said.

President Ali Abdullah Saleh issued a decree endorsing the 28-member cabinet, which will be sworn in on Saturday, a day before the new parliament holds its first session after last month's general elections, officials said.

All but four ministers in the new government are members of Saleh's ruling General People's Congress (GPC) which scored a landslide victory in the polls, the first general elections since a 1994 civil war nearly tore the country apart.
"This shows GPC's commitment to carry out its election programme, including continuing economic reforms...," said one official.
Saleh on Wednesday named Polish-educated Bin Ghanem, 60, to replace Abdul-Aziz Abdul-Ghani, a GPC member. Abdul-Ghani had presented the government's resignation on Monday.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdul-Karim al-Iryani, Interior Minister Hussein Mohammad Arab, Planning and Development Minister Abdul-Qader Bagammal and Industry Minister Ahmed Mohammad Sofan were reappointed.
Newcomers included Mohammad al-Khadem al-Wajih who took over the oil and mineral resources portfolio and Finance Minister Alawi Saleh al-Salami, a former Central Bank governor.

Diplomats said the changes reflected no policy shifts in the impoverished Arab state where unemployment stands at 25 percent. Defence Minister Abdul-Malek al-Sayani was replaced by Mohammad Deifallah Mohammad, television said.

Bin Ghanim eliminated two of three previous posts of deputy prime ministers, separated labour from the social development portfolio and created a new post of minister of state for prime ministry affairs.
Bin Ghanem last served as ambassador to the United Nations in Geneva. He became planning minister in 1990 in Yemen's first cabinet after the north and the south united.

Diplomats said the appointment of Bin Ghanem, who hails from the southern province of Hadramaut, was an attempt to assure residents of the south who have been concerned about life under a northern-dominated government.
Yemen launched tough economic reforms agreed with the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 1995 to lure foreign investments and trim budget deficits.

Yemeni officials have said their economy is improving while central bank assets had risen with reforms, but the country remains one of the Arab world's poorest nations with a per capita GDP of $280 a year.
A small independent oil producer, Yemen pumps around 385,000 barrels per day (bpd), of which 190,000 bpd come from the south.
Saleh said last week his ruling GPC would run the country alone after it captured 187 seats in the 301-member parliament.
The Islah Party, GPC's Islamist junior coalition partner in the outgoing government, won 53 seats. It said it would join the opposition.
Independents won 54 seats and two opposition parties took a total of five seats. Results for two seats have yet to be announced.

In united Yemen's first elections in 1993, the GPC won 123, Islah 62, and the main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP) 56. Independents won 47 seats while the rest went to Baathist and Nasserite parties.

The YSP, some of whose leaders launched a secessionist bid that sparked the civil war, and three other parties boycotted the elections to protest at alleged irregularities. The government denied the charges.
